text.en: Navos's death was not a punishment for a sin but the removal of a life that no longer served its mission, like a worker dismissed for sitting idle even though he stole nothing.
Objects have a mission too: the grape is meant to become wine for Kiddush and zemiros, so Navos's unused vineyard itself accused him and was taken from him.
Music, poetry and marriage share one root: each is a matching of parts that belong together, which is why a chasunah has song and why the vineyard, source of song, is also the place of matches.
That Achav obtained the vineyard proves it held a part of his soul; one who takes his own portion dishonestly would have received it honestly had he waited, and now he loses it.
The same vineyard of song that Achav seized became his path to teshuvah, because song stands next to teshuvah; the rebuke over the vineyard moved him where the fire on Har HaKarmel did not.
The difference between Yirmiyahu's 'from the king of Bavel' and Melachim's 'from the king' reflects hester panim versus revealed Providence: the true King of Bavel is Hashem.
A meal is a guest that traveled from the field through the mill, bakery and store to a person's table, and should be received with kavanah.

The Rav reads Rabbi Yochanan's 'Eliyahu will expound this passage' not as a lack of an answer, since he surely knew Ravina's answer, but as a hint that neveilah and treifah allude to the Erev Rav, whom only Eliyahu will bring to teshuvah.
A bris mila is a small-scale geulah: cutting away the four layers of the orlah parallels subduing the four kingdoms, which is why Eliyahu, the herald of the geulah, is present.
A kashya on a passage of Torah is at the same time a kashya on the Jew whose soul is rooted in that passage, so explaining a difficult text is a way of bringing that Jew to teshuvah.
Eliyahu's role of answering the unresolved questions (Teiku) and his role of bringing Jews to teshuvah are one role, because answering a kashya and repairing a soul are the same act.

Behind every midrash peliah stands a neshama peliah, a concealed soul; one who explains such a midrash reaches a level of gilui Eliyahu, since every good Torah thought is Eliyahu working through one's own body.
The advice to grieve over Yerushalayim when stuck on a kashya is explained by the fact that all Jews together are called Yerushalayim: their teshuvah is its rebuilding, and then the Torah opens.

The proof that the four lepers were Gehazi and his sons is that they were not cured: in a time when Elisha healed even a non-Jew like Naaman, only those under his own eternal curse would remain lepers.

The lepers' words 'this is a day of good tidings and we are silent' express their hope to be cured: since all healing comes from the aspect of Eliyahu, and the bearer of good news receives that aspect, gladdening a whole city could lift the tzaraas.

The Navi records the lepers' full reasoning to show how compelling it was, so that the king's refusal stands out as irrational; his later acceptance of a two-horse search proves the refusal came only so that Gehazi would not become the bearer of good tidings.

The first report reached only 'the house of the king', as if spoken to the walls, because the good tidings of Gehazi were not accepted; the second report, from the searchers, was told to the king himself.
Gehazi, who kept talmidim from Elisha, became measure for measure the teacher of all Klal Yisrael, since the halacha of risking chayei sha'ah for a cure is learned from his words.

The same halacha that Gehazi taught argues for his own return: if a Jewish body is so precious that its healing overrides chayei sha'ah, which itself overrides Shabbos, how much more must one go out of the way to heal a Jewish soul.

The elder trampled on Erev Pesach, a gilgul of the mocking officer, died just before the night of freedom; had he reached Pesach, which like Yovel returns everyone who was pushed away, he would have had his tikkun.
The Rav reads the Gemara's 'until anger' as a sign of success: like a reaction to an inoculation, the anger shows the rebuke has stirred up an inner struggle with the yetzer hara.
Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand parables are explained as three thousand descending levels, each parable explaining the one above it, until his thought reached people's understanding.
The ten levels of holiness parallel the ten utterances of creation, so the Kodesh HaKodashim, the tenth, corresponds to the union of chassan and kallah, which explains the keruvim there.
Matan Torah was the moment the holiness of Shir HaShirim, otherwise confined to the Kodesh HaKodashim, came down into the physical world.
Yishmael and Esav are the refuse of Avraham's chesed and Yitzchak's gevurah, cast off like side effects of a medicine so that Yitzchak and Yaakov could come out pure.
Netzach and hod are the two legs that let a person stand: one by fighting, the other by yielding, like grass that bends in a storm while a stiff tree cracks.
All the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah fall in the sedros read during Sefirah, because these are the kallah's days of holiness and purity.
A mitzvah can have more than one place: just as milah is tied to both Chevron and Shechem, Rosh Hashanah has its place in the Beis Hamikdash and also at the place of Shmuel Hanavi.
'Haras olam', the world's conception on Rosh Hashanah, is mirrored in Chana conceiving Shmuel, the head of the prophets, on that day.
Eli's objection to Chana's long prayer reflects the way tefillah is belittled: learning and giving tzedakah bring honor, while one who davens long is mocked.
Barrenness is read spiritually: a tefillah that is not accepted and learning without success are 'barren', without fruit.
Chana's new name Tzevakos, linked to netzach and hod from which prophecy draws, fits that her son Shmuel began the era of prophecy.
Although the obligation of aliyah l'regel applies only to the three festivals, Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh on Rosh Hashanah too, so Chana's prayer there was a Rosh Hashanah prayer.
Shimshon's apparently improper deeds are explained as a descent to the lowest, assimilating Jews in order to pull them out, done with self-sacrifice for Klal Yisroel.
Hair, which people cut off and which is farthest from the brain, stands for the Jews cut off from Klal Yisroel; Shimshon of Dan, the last tribe, drew his strength from exactly them.
'Nezer Elokav al rosho', said of the nazir's hair, has the gematria of ikvesa d'meshicha: the last Jews are the crown.
Just as hair is the last thing to form in a fetus and shows that it is complete, so the last generation completes Klal Yisroel.
Shimshon was ready to give his life to fight those who harm Hashem's servants, while the Plishtim of today give their lives to harm Jews; the name 'Palestinians' ties them to the Plishtim.

The Rav pairs 'l'shichno sidreshu' with the king 'asher yivchar Hashem': neither the chosen place nor the chosen king is named in the Torah, and only the chosen soul of Dovid could find the chosen place, which is what Doeg recognized and envied.
Yaakov's 'shifchah' is Avigail: since Naval was Lavan reincarnated, Yaakov's restraint toward Lavan was itself the power of Avigail, who taught Dovid to wait until Hashem acted.

Moshiach's soul comes through unlikely and even disreputable channels so the Satan will not notice, and for the same reason the false rumor about Dovid and Bas Sheva was allowed to spread until the Beis HaMikdash was built.

Dovid considered Naval a rebel even before he reigned, because malchus beis Dovid, anointed with Moshe's oil, is a kingship of the Shechinah; Avigail's two arguments answered the ordinary kingship and the heavenly one separately.
'Avigail eishes Naval' equals 'Dovid melech Yisrael chai v'kayam' in gematria: Avigail is the guarantee of Dovid's eternity, the 'Magen Dovid' that protects the point of Dovid.

Sefer Devarim is the last hei of Hashem's name and the esrog among the four species: it stands apart like teshuvah, and the faults at its beginning are the esrog's delicate tip, cleaned in Elul until all sins become merits.
Following Sefer Yetzirah, Elul is Yerushalayim in time: in Elul one enters Yerushalayim, on Rosh Hashanah the Beis HaMikdash, and on Yom Kippur the Kodesh.

Eliyahu's offering 'outside' on Carmel had to take that form: Jews pushed outside the camp by idol worship could only be raised by an offering that was itself outside, and its acceptance showed the door was open to them.

Eliyahu never sinned and needed no atonement; since he lives in the rectified world where Jerusalem reaches Damascus and includes Carmel, his offering and his 'exile' to Damascus only looked like chutz and galus to ordinary eyes.
Mikdash and Damesek are made of the same letters: the two opposites will become one, and out of Damascus, root of tzaraas, Mikdash will come.

Damascus is spelled with a reish only in Divrei Hayamim, the book of completed malchus; reish stands for shalom, the cure for tzaraas, and Damascus with that reish equals 'machaneh Yisroel' in gematria.
A 'teiku' in the Gemara is rooted in a questioned Jew whose letter in the Torah carries a kushya; Eliyahu answers the Gemara's questions by answering the questions on those Jews.
'Mevaser tov' equals Eliyahu, Elisha and Gechazi in gematria: the true good tidings are when Eliyahu comes together with Elisha and the rectified Gechazi.

Torah is not a record of the past: Rebbi refrained from cursing Nevuchadnetzar in ordinary speech yet cursed him while reading Yirmiyahu, because whoever learns a sefer stands in its time, when the wicked king is alive.
The Seder itself shows the makkos are healing for Israel: the very cup from which drops are spilled for the ten makkos is the cup over which Hallel and the geulah are said.
'Bni bechori Yisrael' is Hashem's protest in the sense of chazakah law: as long as the true owner protests, the nations who hold the Jews in galus gain no ownership over them.

Tzidkiyahu imprisoned Yirmiyahu in the hall where Shlomo planned the Beis HaMikdash so that the prophet of calamity, Shlomo's own reincarnation, would receive a prophecy of consolation in Shlomo's merit.

The same place could bring consolation but not annulment: the room where the Beis HaMikdash was planned, on the day Hashem's anger began, is itself the accuser, and an accuser cannot become a defender.

Rashi's first and last Torah frame one message: his first answers the nations who call the Jews thieves of the land, and his last, on chezkas habatim, teaches that the land and the Beis HaMikdash remain the Jews' by Hashem's chazakah.
Shlomo's love for Hashem made him so united with Him that his own name was absorbed into the name of the King to whom peace belongs; the drash of 'Shlomo' is thus the inner meaning of the plain one.
Shir Hashirim and the Holy of Holies share the name kodesh kodashim because both are the place of the chosson and kallah: the keruvim there, the love song here.
Every Yom Tov is a 'chag', a circle, dancing around Shemini Atzeres, which is not called a chag because it is the point in the middle.
Shlomo is the only person who ever reached everything he desired, because his life was a sample of the days of Moshiach, when Hashem too will have full nachas from His world.

The same soul has two sides: Shlomo, who built the Beis HaMikdash and wrote Megillas Shir Hashirim, and Yirmiyahu, who saw its destruction and wrote Megillas Eichah; and 'Shlomo HaMelech' with its letters spelled out equals Tisha B'Av in gematria.
Shlomo stood in the fifteenth generation from Avraham, like the moon full on the fifteenth day, and from him the generations declined to the destruction in the thirtieth.
Shlomo is Hashem's appointed poet, and Klal Yisrael also appointed him as theirs, so the songs of Shir Hashirim run back and forth between the chosson and the kallah.

Following Reb Feivel, the Rav explains the Midrash that the nations who sacrifice in the north will be uprooted while Klal Yisrael, who sacrifice in the south, will come: olos are slaughtered in the north and a gentile can bring only an olah, while a Jew's shelamim, slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard and eaten, shows his power to sanctify the physical.

Shir Hashirim is holy of holies precisely because it takes the most physical relationship, chassan and kallah, as the mashal for Hashem and Klal Yisrael; until Shlomo it was not known that this world holds sparks of holiness that can be raised, and that is why Rabbi Akiva said the world was never as worthy as on the day it was given.

The tenth in every set of ten concerns chassan and kallah: in the ten maamaros it is 'it is not good for man to be alone', the tenth dibbur 'lo sachmod' means a person should have his own kallah and not covet another's, and Avraham's tenth trial, the Akeidah, brought about Yitzchak's zivug.

Shlomo's name reflects his place as the fifteenth generation, the full moon of Klal Yisrael; precisely because he stood at the peak and knew the waning would begin after him, he addressed Shir Hashirim to the darkness of the moon in galus.

Every neshamah owns a portion of Torah that only it can reveal; therefore Hashem could say the halachah of the parah adumah at Sinai in Rabbi Eliezer's name, Adam's 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' belongs to Dovid's soul, and Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo even though it was sung at the sea and at Sinai.

Yayin has the numerical value of seventy: Klal Yisrael's answer to the nations who invite them to live like gentiles and escape persecution is that Hashem's love is better than all the 'wine' of the seventy nations.
The Rav reads the 'kiss' of the pasuk as the Shechinah resting on a Jew's lips and speaking out of his mouth when he says words of Torah or tefillah.
He explains why the Oral Torah is dearer: the Written Torah comes down from Heaven to the world, while the Oral Torah is renewed by Jews below and is received above.
He uses the halachah of hashakah, where water in a vessel touching a mikveh becomes mikveh water, to explain how learning makes a Jew part of Hashem.
He reads Shlomo HaMelech's sixty warriors as the sixty masechtos, so that his army, and the Jewish people's defense ever since, is the Torah.
Shemen, oil, hints at shemoneh, eight, above the seven of nature; therefore the Chanukah miracle came through oil and lasted eight days.
In Tehillim 19 the first seven pesukim speak of nature, and the eighth, 'Toras Hashem temimah', speaks of Torah, which is above nature.
Hitler hated even assimilated Jews who lived like Germans, which the Rav says shows that the nations know Israel is the chosen people.
Oil makes no sound when it is poured, unlike water or wine, and so Hashem's 'oil', His miracles, His tzaddikim and the good deeds of every Jew, works quietly and in hiding.
Just as a drop of water poured into a full glass of oil pushes out a drop of oil, a word of foolishness that a person says or hears pushes out a drop of Torah.

The Rambam's Moshiach, who shows no wonders but draws the whole people after him and brings them to Eretz Yisrael, is greater than a wonder-working Moshiach, since moving every heart is the greatest miracle.

Following the Yismach Moshe, the first 'ad ya'avor' in the pasuk carries Hashem's Name and so could not be lost, while the second does not, which is why sin could hold back the miracles of the Second Beis Hamikdash.
The Chanukah light is lit below ten tefachim, in the public domain, at night, in the darkest season, because Moshiach will come down to the lowest place of the Jewish people and lift them from there.
The Rav reads 'alamos' in the pasuk as coming from 'he'elem', concealment: the fragrance of the old miracles is what keeps Jews loving Hashem even when He hides His face.

The Rav reads the Chanukah war as a war of Jews against Jews, and sees the same pattern in Russia and in the fight of Reform and Conservative against Torah Jews; the Chafetz Chaim held that a fight against the Yevsektsia, like the war against the Greeks, would have succeeded.
One year in the years of youth is worth many years later on, when a person has reached a plateau and no longer grows.
A kulah is suspect not because it is false but because its motive may be hidden: a person who calls a remote danger a reason to skip davening would not say so about going to a party.
Gerim are Jewish souls born among goyim; their restless drive is what brings them back to their root, and they 'smell' the miracles that other nations ignore.

Galus is the time of the greatest revelations of Torah: Rabbi Akiva's secrets, Yechezkel's Merkavah, and the Talmud Bavli, which Eretz Yisroel's sages did not merit to develop, all came in galus out of Hashem's compassion.
The words with which Yechezkel describes seeing the heavens open spell emunah: whoever is not granted the vision must believe it.
Following the Midrash, Shlomo HaMelech's 'we will rejoice in You' settles the ambiguity of 'in it' in Hallel: the joy of the day is joy in Hashem Himself.
The 'love more than wine' of the verse is the halachos of each Yom Tov, learned in its time: they put more warmth into a Jew's blood than wine does.
Because the Jewish people cannot exist without the moadim, and the fixed calendar depends on Jews in Eretz Yisrael, Hashem saw to it that Jews never ceased to live there through all its conquerors.
Shabbos is an oasis where a weary traveler stops to rest; Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals, are a jump-start that lets a Jew keep moving in the midst of galus.
Physical pleasure ends in satiation, but on Shabbos a Jew can be fully sated and still delight, because his soul is bound to Hashem.
The wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos but fit for Chanukah are souls too extinguished to burn on Shabbos, which can be kindled on Chanukah because then the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim.
Weekdays, 'chol', are like illness, 'choleh'; the Chanukah lights are Hashem's house call, the Shechinah coming down to visit the sick.
The proof that a Jew is good in essence is that like begets like: since he comes from the Avos, he is essentially as they were, and his sins are only incidental.
Teshuvah means returning to one's roots; a Jew has good roots to return to, while for a gentile, whose sin is essential, it does not help in the same way.
Hashem's answer to 'is not Esav a brother to Yaakov' is that even when their deeds look alike, Esav is bad in essence and Yaakov good in essence.
Shabbos is not only a taste of Olam Haba: following Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin, it is the fountain from which Olam Haba itself draws.
The word 'Shabbos' means return: on Shabbos the soul goes back to the Kisei HaKavod it was hewn from, where no sin reaches, which unites the two Midrashim on 'black but beautiful'.
Weekdays ('chol') are like sickness ('choleh'), prison, desert and sea; Shabbos is the release for which the four who must give thanks in Hodu thank Hashem.
Checking one's garments ('begadim') on Erev Shabbos is read, in the Slonimer Rebbes' Chassidic interpretation, as checking one's betrayals ('bgidos') against Hashem and doing teshuvah.

Eliyahu's forbidden offering outside on Har HaCarmel was itself the descent of the tzaddik: like a korban slaughtered outside, he reached the souls outside the camp of Israel, and that is why he then needed atonement and exile.

From Eliyahu's own standpoint the offering was not outside at all: Har HaCarmel will be inside the future Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash will stand there, so he already stood in the Yerushalayim of the world of tikkun.

The dispute over Gechazi resolves in the future: a metzora cannot enter Yerushalayim, but when Yerushalayim spreads to Damascus, the seat of tzaraas, the outcasts there will find themselves inside the camp of Israel.

Divrei HaYamim, the last book of Tanach which completes malchus and leans toward the world of tikkun, spells Damascus 'Darmesek', with a reish that equals machaneh Yisrael, and spells David with a yud as it will be in the redemption.

Because every Jew is a letter in the Torah, a kushya in the Torah is a kushya on some Jew; one who toils to answer a hard Gemara or Tosafos brings teshuvah to that Jew, and this is the deeper meaning of 'Tishbi will answer the kushyos'.
Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the highest gilui Eliyahu is when Eliyahu comes with Elisha and Gechazi runs after them; in the end Gechazi will catch up, so that all Jews reach their tikkun.
The small avodah of the lowest generation is like the cheap pearl brought from the depths of the sea: it proves the King's reign reaches even there, and so it is set at the head of the crown.
Following a rule that whatever the Gemara brings in, even incidentally, belongs to its sugya, the Rav reads the long Avigail story as part of the meaning of Purim.

The yom tov was not accepted because the Megillah, written with ruach hakodesh, speaks of the King, Hashem, and of the final war with Amalek; the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah understood that its full yom tov belongs to the final redemption.

Because the Satan fears the kingdom of David, it always emerges through roots that invite talk, like Rus the Moabite and Bas Sheva, so that he will not suspect it; David himself caused the talk on purpose.
Avigail's 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah' was her answer to David's thought that Moshiach would come from her: the kingdom would come through Bas Sheva, not through her.

Avigail the wife of David equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, and the missing yud in her name shows the missing malchus: she is the aspect of Purim, the beginning of the kingdom that is completed at Pesach.
Eliyahu is called a kohen not by lineage but because, as the herald of the redemption, he always lives in the state of the days of Moshiach, when every Jew will be a kohen.
Eliyahu's answer that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon was not a mere deflection for him: in the future the halacha will follow Rabbi Shimon, and Eliyahu already lives in that time.
Rabbi Shimon is not followed now because he is on the level of Shabbos, the whole year Shabbos for him, a level the world has not yet reached.
Since lighting Chanukah candles reveals the light of Moshiach as a returning light, not only does the home become a Beis HaMikdash but the Jew himself becomes a kohen.
Hereditary office is not a social arrangement: because kingship is Hashem's alone and His kingship is 'in every generation', a king who is a vessel for it must pass it on to his son.

The Rav distinguishes kingship from service: the bigger Eisav's nation, the more its ruler is their servant, and likewise a chazan appointed only temporarily is a servant, so the Rema's condition does not contradict the Torah's promise of inheritance.

Before David received the promise, Moshiach could come from any tribe; Shaul reigned exactly when Edom's eight kings had passed, so he could have been the one, which the Rav sees hinted in a gematria linking Shiloh and Shaul.

From the Targum that Shaul counted the people by their Pesach lambs, the Rav concludes that his war on Amalek fell on the eve of Pesach, the destined time, so delaying by even a day meant the chance was gone.

Shaul did not dispute Shmuel's prophecy, only his halachic ruling, and was entitled to his own reasoning; his failure was that the war against Amalek, the opposite of self-nullification, required him to yield to the elder of the generation.
Esther is the counterpart of Shaul: as queen she still obeyed Mordechai as she had as a girl, and that self-nullification is what let her prevail over Haman.
Purim's meal falls on a weekday because its task is to elevate kelipas nogah, which cannot be done on Shabbos and which only a Jew, not a gentile, can raise to holiness.
